Michael Jackson’s Surprising Connection To Michigan’s Adventure

Tommy McNeillPublished: August 10, 2026
  • Share on Facebook
  • Share on Twitter
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 2:12
Instaread

A rite of passage here in West Michigan is taking a trip to Michigan's Adventure. I still remember the first time I worked up the nerve to finally ride Shivering Timbers, one of the world's largest wooden roller coasters; when I stepped off, I had a chest full of hair, and my voice had dropped three octaves.

Get our free mobile app

Okay, not really, but the park has been a fixture in Muskegon and has changed drastically since its days as Deer Park in the 1950s, and that is because of the attractions it has added over the years.

But one of its rides has some lore that few know about, largely because it centers on why it was removed from the park, and it involves the King of Pop himself.

From Michigan's Adventure to Neverland

Michael Jackson, the "King of Pop," who consistently broke Billboard records and had 13 No. 1 hits throughout his solo career, was known for his eccentricness as much as his music. That was most prominently seen in his massive Neverland Ranch homestead in California that he turned into a fantasy-themed amusement park throughout the 90s, complete with a petting zoo and over 18 rides.

These rides included Ferris wheels and merry-go-rounds, and more intense rides like a Sea Dragon and the Zipper (Michael's favorite). As it turns out, one of those 18 rides was purchased from Michigan's Adventure: the Eyerly Spider. It was a ride that raised and lowered riders while spinning them around on 6 (not 8, despite its name) arms. You can actually see the Spider in this tour video of Neverland at the 2:25 mark.

Michael Jackson's Neverland Theater and Amusement Park Tour 1993

What Happened To Michael's Spider Ride?

The downfall of Neverland Ranch is unfortunately very documented, on account of the allegations of Jackson's inappropriate relationship with a child. After he was acquitted in 2005, Michael vowed to never visit it again. Thus, after his death a few years later, all the amusement rides were sold off.

READ MORE: Boblo Island: The History of Detroit’s Beloved Amusement Park

Parkworld Online reports that David Helm of Helm & Sons Amusements purchased the  Crown steam train, CP Huntington train, Carousel, Spider, Slide, and Wave Swinger. This was as of 2009, so its whereabouts today are unknown.

Either way, it's still an interesting tidbit that something as random as a Spider ride from Muskegon could end up in the backyard of Michael Jackson.

Michigan's Forgotten Amusement and Theme Parks

Michigan's Adventure wasn't always the only game in town. Here's a look back at the amusement parks that came before it.

Gallery Credit: Tommy McNeill

Stephens Home Movies via YouTube

Deer Park - Muskegon

Let's start with the park that I mentioned earlier, which would one day become Michigan's Adventure. In its early days, Michigan's Adventure was merely a petting zoo with its only "attraction" area being a place called Storybook Lane.

As the park began adding rides, starting with the Deer Park Special in 1958, it rebranded as Deer Park Funland. The final rebrand happened in 1988 to Michigan's Adventure.

Ephemerania via eBay

Pleasure Park - Muskegon

These days, Michigan's Adventure is known for both its roller coasters and expansive water park, but that wasn't always the case. For many years, Pleasure Park was the go-to place for people to cool down on hot days. Opened in the early 1980s, this water park had a variety of waterslides, a mini golf course, and more, with the Black Hole water slide and the Twister being its most popular attractions.

For many years, Michigan's Adventure and Pleasure Park co-existed, but when Michigan's Adventure added its WildWater Adventure water park in 1990, it turned out Muskegon wasn't big enough for two water parks, and Pleasure Park couldn't compete. It closed and was put up for auction in 1997

Photo credit: Ephemerania via eBay

Ruin Road via YouTube

Deer Forest - Coloma

Not to be mistaken for a different deer-themed park on this list, Deer Forest was a theme park open from 1949 to 2014. A petting zoo/amusement park, it allowed families to feed animals like deer and antelope and featured various rides, such as a Ferris wheel, which entertained families for over 60 years.

The property sat vacant for years, with many buildings and pieces of equipment left to decay. The 21-acre property was put up for auction in 2021.


Photo by Lizgrin F on Unsplash

Oakwood Amusement Park - Kalamazoo

*Note: The photo is not of the Oakwood Amusement Park; the photo is used for reference. To view photos of the amusement park, click here.

The Oakwood Amusement Park, once called Kalamazoo's Coney Island, was around from 1893 to 1925. It had many different iterations, changing names multiple times before settling on Oakwood Park. What started as a place to dance, ride merry-go-rounds, and fly hot air balloons turned into a place for theater (including the famous film The Great Train Robbery) and eventually became a proper amusement park

It was buoyed by the "Dizzy Figure-8" roller coaster until it closed in 1925 after attendance declined and a performer died. Nothing remains of the park today, though construction in the area tends to unearth artifacts. Read more about the park's history.

Detroit Historical Society

Boblo Island - Detroit

A short ferry ride from Detroit was Boblo Island, an island with roller coasters, ferris wheels, spinning gondolas, dance halls, and more. Each guest was greeted by Bobbie the Bear and Louie the Lion.

It opened in 1898 and was open for nearly 100 years before closing in 1993. Now, houses stand where the park once stood. You can read more here.

WyantSteve via YouTube

Silver Beach Amusement Park - St. Joseph

One thing that hasn't changed about Michiganders is how we cool off on a hot day. Going to the lake has been the way to spend a summer day. This led to Silver Beach Amusement Park being created on the shores of Lake Michigan in 1891, providing access to roller coasters (most notably the Velvet Coaster), a merry-go-round that is still an important part of St. Joseph history, and a carnival that draws thousands each year, creating the ultimate beach day.

But according to WOODTV 8, the amusement park couldn't keep up with improving technology like air conditioning, crime spiraled out of control, and bigger parks in the area eventually led to its demise in 1972.

msdcards via eBay

Tashmoo Park - Detroit

Located on Harsens Island in the St. Clair Flats from 1897 to 1951, Tashmoo Park was a popular park that featured a casino, dance pavilion, roller rink, recreation center, and sports area. But while those were normal for amusement parks of the era, the steamship that brought guests there was almost as much of an experience as any other attraction.

Pictured above is the massive Tashmoo, a 306-foot steamship named after the park that could carry 3,500 passengers at a time and was the largest paddle-wheeled steamboat on the Great Lakes. Taking a ride on this huge boat was the mode of transport to the island and provided stunning views of the area around it.

However, a fatal collision with a rock, the Great Depression, and the invention of the automobile all led to a decline in visitors to Tashmoo, and it eventually closed.
Photo credit: msdcards via eBay.

The Flipping Bro via eBay

Cereal City, U.S.A. - Battle Creek

The birthplace of cereal, Battle Creek, once embraced its moniker of "Cereal City" by creating "Cereal City, U.S.A." In 1998, Kellogg's opened a massive $22 million, 45,000 square-foot family attraction that was a "cross between a factory tour and a theme park", letting kids meet the cereal characters they saw on TV and cereal boxes while also learning how cereal was made via a (fake) cereal production line.

However, while the concept seemed like a home run given the success of their factory tours, it never reached the necessary attendance and closed in 2007, only 10 years after opening.

Photo credit: The Flipping Bro via eBay

Grand Rapids City Clerk's Office, “Postcard of the Derby Racer at Ramona Park,” City of Grand Rapids Archives and Records Center, accessed August 9, 2026, https://grandrapidsmicityarchives.omeka.net/items/show/838.

Ramona Park - Grand Rapids

Ramonda Park and the Ramona resort operated in East Grand Rapids on Reed's Lake from 1886 to 1954. Per the Michigan Historical site plaque located at Wealthy St. and Lake Dr.:

"For many West Michigan residents - including President Gerald R. Ford, who recalled Babe Ruth and the New York Yankees playing a Grand Rapids minor league baseball team at Ramona Ball Park, the park was a place for fond memories that included hot-air balloon ascensions on Sunday Afternoons and steamboat trips around Reeds Lake.

By the late 1940s, new entertainment options and a declining need for public transportation decreased park attendance. Desiring a new use for the area, the community called for the park's removal. Its last season was in 1954."

As shown in the postcard, the park had a large wooden roller coaster, as well as an outdoor amphitheater, merry-go-round, a Ferris wheel, a ballpark, and more. The Park's beloved organ, Big Bertha, is on display in another theme park known around the world: the Grand Floridian hotel at Disney World, per WOODTV 8.

UpNorth Memories Collection via eBay

Wenoa Beach Amusement Park - Bay City

Bay City was once home to Wenoa Beach Amusement Park, Michigan's oldest park. From 1887 to 1964, this park on Wenoa Beach treated beachgoers to dancing, boardwalks, boating, and a roller coaster known as the Jack Rabbit, according to Michigan Blue.

According to Thumbwind, the decline of this park wasn't like the others listed above. Other parks battled declining attendance because of technology or social changes. Wenoa Beach struggled because of a snowstorm in 1947 that destroyed the bathhouse and roller coaster shown above. While the park attempted to recover from this, it never did.

It closed its doors for good in 1964.

pedrothefish via eBay

Lake Michigan Park - Muskegon

This beachside amusement park differs from the others. In terms of attractions and amenities, it is similar: a Ferris wheel, roller coaster, bathhouse, theater, etc. But what made this park unique, to a fault as we'll learn, was its reliance on the train.

The train, from the beginning in 1890, was central to the park. It and the park were owned by Muskegon Traction and Lighting Company. It brought guests to the beach and, thus, to the park. While this worked for many years, once again the invention of the streetcar and the need to no longer use the train eventually led to this park's downfall around the 1930s.

Photo credit: pedrothefish via eBay

Lakeland Amusement Park, Houghton Lake
